sections.title: Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Components
sections.en: 14.3.2 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Components The five components of DDMRP (see Figure 14.4) show a materials planner how to effec- tively position buffers at strategic inventory locations, protect the flow of materials and relevant information by evaluating buffer profiles, and then dynamically adjust these buffers. Finally, an efficient pull system is put in place to reduce variability between demand and supply through demand-driven planning. Figure 14.4 Five Components of DDMRP (©Demand Driven Institute, Used with Permission) This is followed by execution while ensuring that the changing supply and demand dynamics adapt to the logistics and supply chain. Demand Driven Material Requirements Planning Strategic Inventory Positioning Buffer Profiles and Levels Dynamic Adjustments Demand Driven Planning Visible and Collaborative Execution Position 1 Protect 2 3 Pull 4 5 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 778 Strategic Inventory Positioning In this component (see Figure 14.4), a materials planner decides which items to stock and where. Materials that are prime candidates for consideration are those with long lead times, significant supply or demand variability, or a component used in manufac- turing several products, plus those that face a production capacity bottleneck. The planner chooses materials from the stock buffers as well as the decoupling points in the logistics and supply chain. As already covered previously, the buffers at decoupling points are denoted by the icon. The following two questions will immediately arise in your mind when you’re choos- ing a decoupling point:  What important factors should I consider while selecting a decoupling point in the logistics and supply chain?  Where should I position a decoupling point in the logistics and supply chain? The six factors you should consider when choosing a decoupling point are as follows:  Customer tolerance time The maximum amount of time customers are willing to wait for delivery or avail- ability of a product before seeking alternatives  Market potential lead time Lead time that will allow an increase in price or an opportunity to capture additional business through existing or new customer channels  Demand or sales order visibility horizon The time period during which the demand for dependent requirements is known or when there’s visibility into actual sale of products as recorded in a sales order  External variabilities – Demand variability The probability of spikes and swings in demand that may overwhelm resources such as capacity, stock, and cash flow – Supply variability The potential for and probability of supply disruptions from specific sources of supply (suppliers or interplant transfers)  Inventory leverage and flexibility The specific places in an integrated BOM structure that enable a company to have maximum options for product availability and the best lead time compression  Critical operation protection Putting specific control points in place to minimize potential points of disruptions in the supply chain, such as placing control points at work centers or production resources with bottleneck capacities or where demand/supply variabilities can quickly accumulate or amplify © 779 14.3 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Basics and Components Based on these six factors for choosing decoupling points, Figure 14.5 shows an exam- ple of strategically placed buffers. These buffers are based on the following consider- ations:  The FPG and 201 buffers let you quickly take advantage of additional business oppor- tunities.  The FPG stock position is minimized due to the 101 buffer.  The 101 and 102P buffers allow for an MTO strategy on FPH.  The 201 and 204P buffers protect the Z resource as best as possible at the product structure (BOM) level.  The 301P buffer minimizes the inventory liability at 201.  The 201 and 101 buffers can direct the shared components to actual requirements. Figure 14.5 Strategically Placed Buffers (©Demand Driven Institute, Used with Permission) The following are the six tests you should consider when evaluating a decoupling point:  Decoupling test The lead time on the supply side should decrease when compared with the lead time chain of the nonbuffered components.  Bidirectional benefit test The demand side should show a compressed or reduced lead time and higher avail- ability of a product or a component. The supply side should get cumulative demand requirements to provide a materials planner with better and more efficient order management of the recommended order quantity.  Order independence test The stock in the buffers isn’t specific to any production order, sales order, or stock transport order (interplant transfer). This test therefore ensures that there’s as little WIP as possible while making stock available for any demand. 30 Days 20 Days 3 Days 2 Days 2 Days 5 Days 10 Days 204P 201 101 FPG FPH Z C E F C C C C B A B T S T S 102P 301P 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 780  Primary planning mechanism test The buffered part at a decoupling point should be able to manage all demand and supply requirements independently by taking the net flow position into account.  Relative priority test The buffered position needs to account for both planning and execution of not just the buffered part but also its priority in relation to other buffered parts and posi- tions.  Dynamic adjustment test The buffered part needs to adjust dynamically to account for supply and demand variations within the defined time horizon. Buffer Profiles and Levels In this component (see Figure 14.4), you as a materials planner decide how much stock to hold (the buffers) at specific decoupling points. You group together materials that share similar characteristics and attributes (e.g., raw or packing materials with long lead times, finished goods with high demand variability, several intermediate products sharing a common machine or a bottlenecked work center) and then assign them rele- vant buffer profiles. Then, you maintain buffer levels. Let’s take a look at the three buffer zones (red, yellow, and green) and how to calculate them (see Figure 14.6). You calculate the yellow zone 1, and then the green zone 2, and finally the red zone 3.  Yellow zone This is central to the demand coverage in the buffer, and you calculate it using the following formula: Average daily usage (ADU) × Decoupled lead time (DLT)  Green zone This determines the order frequency and the size of each order. There are three ways to calculate the green zone, and the largest value of the three calculations forms the green buffer zone: – Minimum order quantity (MOQ) – Desired order cycle (DOC) × DLT – ADU × DLT × Lead time factor (LT factor)  Red zone This is the embedded safety in the buffer. The red zone is the sum of the red zone base and the red zone safety, as follows: – Red zone base: ADU × DLT × LT factor – Red zone safety: Red zone base × Variability factor (VF) – Red zone = Red zone base + Red zone safety © 781 14.3 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Basics and Components Figure 14.6 Buffer Zones (©Demand Driven Institute, Used with Permission) To get a better sense of buffer positions, consider the following four abbreviations and their meanings:  Top of red (TOR) This is the highest point of the red zone. When the stock, schedule, or capacity breaches the red zone, it signals the need for urgent action or immediate attention.  Top of yellow (TOY) This is the highest point of the yellow zone. Breaching TOY signals a warning of a buffer situation. TOY = Red zone + Yellow zone.  Top of green (TOG) This is the highest point of the green zone that reflects a comfortable buffer position until it crosses into the TOY zone. TOG = Red + Yellow + Green.  Over the top of green (OTOG) This is a situation in which the on-hand or available stock is over the top of the defined green zone (the TOG), and it signals an excess inventory position. Figure 14.7 shows an example of calculating the buffer zones. You start by calculating the yellow zone, and then you calculate the green zone, and finally the red zone. The data required for calculating all three zones is also shown in Figure 14.7. The three zones are calculated as follows: 1. TOR: 90 2. TOY: Red + Yellow = 90 + 150 = 240 3. TOG: Red + Yellow + Green = 90 + 150 + 90 = 330 Red Zone Base Red Zone Safety Yellow Green Green Zone: Determines supply order generation frequency and size – the largest quantity of either of the following three: • Minimum Order Quantity (MOQ) • Desired Order Cycle (DOC) x Decoupled Lead Time (DLT) • Average Daily Usage (ADU) x Decoupled Lead Time (DLT) x Lead Time (LT) Factor Yellow Zone: The heart of the demand coverage in the buffer • ADU x Decoupled Lead Time (DLT) Red Zone: The embedded safety in the buffer • Red Zone Base: DLT x ADU x LT Factor • Red Zone Safety: Red Zone Base x Variability Factor (VF) • Total Red Zone = Red Zone Base + Red Zone Safety Top of Yellow (TOY) Top of Red (TOR) Top of Green (TOG) Over the Top of Green (OTOG) Blue 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 782 Figure 14.7 Buffer Calculation (©Demand Driven Institute, Used with Permission) Dynamic Adjustments In this component (see Figure 14.4), a materials planner oversees dynamic adjustments to buffers to account for product seasonality, the stage of a product maturity (such as a soon-to-be-discontinued product or a new product introduction), and capacity adjust- ments, and then, the planner prebuilds the requirements in anticipation of future demand or slowdown. Buffers, such as stock buffers, also adjust dynamically to account for supply variability, a procurement or production schedule mismatch, or a machine reaching an overload capacity situation. As already covered, the stock, schedule, and capacity buffers adjust dynamically to ensure elimination of distortions of relevant information and materials flows. Demand-Driven Planning In this component (see Figure 14.4), a materials planner uses the visual planning tools to create replenishment orders where necessary. Replenishment orders are created based on the net flow equation: Net flow equation: On hand + On order – Qualified sales order (or demand) In this equation, on hand is the available stock in the warehouse, on order refers to the quantities of materials ordered and awaiting receipt, and qualified sales order (or demand) refers to sales orders that are due today, those that are past due, and qualified future spikes. The qualified future spike considers the quantity threshold within a defined time horizon in a daily time bucket to decide if the spike qualifies to be included in net flow equation calculation. For example, a qualified future spike is included in the Part Buffer Calculation – An Example Average Daily Usage (ADU) 15 Green Zone 90 (the largest of three calculated values) Buffer Profile (Manufactured, Medium Lead Time, Low Variability) M, M (0.4), L (0.33) LT Factor: 60 (DLT (10)x ADU (15) x Lead Time Factor (0.4)) MOQ (Minimum Order Quantity) 50 Minimum Order Quantity: 50 Imposed or Desired Order Cycle (DOC) 6 days Order Cycle: 90 (6(DOC) x 15(ADU)) Decoupled Lead Time (DLT) 10 days Yellow Zone 150 (10(DLT) x 15(ADU)) Lead Time Factor (M) = 0.4 Variability Factor (L) = 0.33 Red Zone 90 (Red Base (60) + Red Safety (30)) Red Base: 60 (DLT (10)x ADU (15) x Lead Time Factor (0.4)) Red Safety: 30 (Red Base (90) x Variability Factor (0.33)) 120 150 90 0 50 100 150 200 250 300 350 400 90 150 90 © 783 14.3 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Basics and Components net flow equation calculation when the demand quantity of the material is 50 units or more (the quantity threshold) on a single day (in a daily time bucket) and within the time horizon of one week. Visible and Collaborative Execution In this component (see Figure 14.8), you as a materials planner take action to convert suggested replenishment orders into procurement orders, production orders, or stock transport orders. Furthermore, you use material lead times or scheduling synchroniza- tion alerts to quickly attend to any material or scheduling disruptions that threaten to destabilize the supply chain. DDR is a priority-based pull system that alerts planners visually whenever a situation warrants action or attention. Figure 14.8 DDMRP Execution (©Demand Driven Institute, Used with Permission) Table 14.1 shows the DDMRP components mapped to the available DDR apps in SAP S/4HANA. The following is a brief introduction to each component, and we’ll dive into them further in later sections:  Buffer positioning DDMRP starts with the product classification using the Schedule Product Classifica- tion app. After the classification, you can use the Buffer Positioning app to choose where to position the decoupling point buffers. Finally, you classify the products Highly Visible Open Supply Priority Management …NOT priority by due date! Order # Order Type Due Date Customer MO 12379 MTO May - 12 Super Tech MO 12401 12% RED MTS May - 14 Internal MO 12465 27% RED MTS May - 12 Internal MO 12367 53% YELLOW MTS May - 12 Internal MO 12411 61% YELLOW MTS May - 16 Internal Order # Order Type Due Date Customer MO 12367 MTS May - 12 Internal MO 12379 MTO May - 12 Super Tech MO 12465 MTS May - 12 Internal MO 12401 MTS May - 14 Internal MO 12411 MTS May - 16 Internal Order # On-Hand Buffer Status PO 819-87 27% (RED) WO 832-41 42% (RED) WO 211-72 88% (YELLOW) Priority by buffer status… 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 784 according to the lead time using the Schedule Lead Time Classification of Products app. Alternatively, you can manually classify the products using the Mass Mainte- nance of Products (DD) app.  Buffer sizing In this step, you execute the actual buffer calculation with the Schedule Buffer Pro- posal Calculation app. You can also review the calculated buffers by using the Man- age Buffer Levels app.  Replenishment planning You use the Replenishment Planning by Planning Priority app to evaluate which products are below the reorder point.  Replenishment execution You use the Replenishment Execution by On-Hand Status app to check for which products the on-hand stock can’t cover the buffer and thus for which products to expedite the supply.  Analytics This is the last step of the DDMRP process. With the Planned Overview app, you can find the DDMRP-related KPIs, take action, and prevent problems. DDMRP Components DDMRP Component Descriptions DDR Apps in SAP S/4HANA Functionalities of DDR App 1 Strategic inventory positioning Schedule Product Classification (DD) This performs classification (ABC, EFG, and PQR). Manage Buffer Levels This enables users to adjust calculated values of buffers. Table 14.1 DDMRP Components Mapping with DDR Apps in SAP S/4HANA © 785
sections.he:
חמשת רכיבי DDMRP (Figure 14.4) מראים כיצד למקם buffers, להגן על הזרימה בהערכת buffer profiles, ולהתאימם דינמית — ואז pull system יעיל להפחתת שונות. הרכיבים: (1) Position; ‏(2) Protect; ‏(3) Protect; ‏(4) Pull; ‏(5) Pull.

**1. מיקום מלאי אסטרטגי (Strategic Inventory Positioning):** המתכנן מחליט מה ואיפה לאחסן. מועמדים — חומרים עם lead time ארוך, שונות משמעותית, רכיב משותף למספר מוצרים, ובקבוק קיבולת. שתי שאלות בבחירת decoupling point: אילו גורמים לשקול? איפה למקם?
שישה גורמים:
• **Customer tolerance time:** הזמן המקסימלי שהלקוח מוכן לחכות.
• **Market potential lead time:** lead time המאפשר העלאת מחיר או לכידת עסקים נוספים.
• **Demand/sales order visibility horizon:** התקופה שבה הביקוש ידוע או יש נראות למכירה בפועל.
• **External variabilities:** שונות ביקוש (ספייקים) ושונות היצע (שיבושי אספקה).
• **Inventory leverage and flexibility:** המקומות ב-BOM המשולב המאפשרים מקסימום אפשרויות זמינות ודחיסת lead time.
• **Critical operation protection:** נקודות בקרה למזעור שיבושים (במרכזי בקבוק או היכן שהשונות מצטברת).
(Figure 14.5 — buffers ממוקמים: ‏FPG ו-201 ללכידת עסקים; מלאי FPG ממוזער ע"י 101; ‏101 ו-102P מאפשרים MTO על FPH; ‏201 ו-204P מגנים על משאב Z; ‏301P ממזער חבות מלאי ב-201; ‏201 ו-101 מכוונים רכיבים משותפים לדרישות.)
שישה מבחנים להערכת decoupling point:
• **Decoupling test:** ה-lead time בצד ההיצע צריך לקטון מול שרשרת הרכיבים הלא-buffered.
• **Bidirectional benefit test:** צד הביקוש — lead time מצומצם וזמינות גבוהה; צד ההיצע — דרישות מצטברות לניהול הזמנות יעיל.
• **Order independence test:** המלאי ב-buffers אינו ספציפי לכל הזמנה — מינימום WIP תוך זמינות לכל ביקוש.
• **Primary planning mechanism test:** החלק ב-decoupling point צריך לנהל את כל הדרישות עצמאית לפי net flow position.
• **Relative priority test:** עדיפות החלק ביחס לאחרים.
• **Dynamic adjustment test:** התאמה דינמית לשונות באופק.

**2. פרופילי ורמות Buffer (Buffer Profiles and Levels):** המתכנן מחליט כמה מלאי (buffers) להחזיק. מקבצים חומרים בעלי מאפיינים דומים (גלם/אריזה עם lead time ארוך, גמורים עם שונות גבוהה, ביניים החולקים מכונה/בקבוק) ומקצים buffer profiles, ואז רמות. שלושה אזורים (red, yellow, green; ‏Figure 14.6) — מחשבים צהוב, אז ירוק, אז אדום:
• **אזור צהוב (Yellow):** לב כיסוי הביקוש: `ADU × DLT` (ממוצע צריכה יומית × decoupled lead time).
• **אזור ירוק (Green):** קובע תדירות וגודל הזמנה. הגדול מבין שלושה: ‏MOQ (minimum order quantity); ‏DOC × DLT (desired order cycle); ‏ADU × DLT × LT factor.
• **אזור אדום (Red):** הבטיחות המוטמעת. סכום ה-base וה-safety: ‏Red base = ADU × DLT × LT factor; ‏Red safety = Red base × VF (variability factor); ‏Red = base + safety.
מיקומי buffer:
• **TOR (Top of red):** הנקודה הגבוהה של האדום. שבירה → פעולה דחופה.
• **TOY (Top of yellow):** ‏Red + Yellow. שבירה → אזהרה.
• **TOG (Top of green):** ‏Red + Yellow + Green. מצב נוח.
• **OTOG (Over the top of green):** המלאי מעל ה-TOG → עודף מלאי.
(Figure 14.7 — דוגמת חישוב: ‏ADU 15, ‏profile (M, M=0.4, L=0.33), ‏MOQ 50, ‏DOC 6 ימים, ‏DLT 10 ימים, ‏LT Factor 0.4, ‏VF 0.33. ‏Green 90 (הגדול מ-3: ‏60, ‏MOQ 50, ‏order cycle 90); ‏Yellow 150 (10 × 15); ‏Red 90 (base 60 + safety 30). ‏TOR 90; ‏TOY 240 (90+150); ‏TOG 330 (90+150+90).)

**3. התאמות דינמיות (Dynamic Adjustments):** המתכנן מתאים buffers לעונתיות, בגרות מוצר (לקראת הפסקה או השקה), והתאמות קיבולת, ובונה-מראש לציפייה. ‏buffers מתאימים דינמית לשונות היצע, אי-התאמת תזמון, או עומס מכונה.

**4. תכנון מבוסס-ביקוש (Demand-Driven Planning):** המתכנן יוצר הזמנות חידוש לפי נוסחת ה-net flow:
`net flow = on hand + on order − qualified sales order (ביקוש)`
‏on hand = מלאי זמין; ‏on order = הוזמן וממתין; ‏qualified = הזמנות להיום, באיחור, וספייקים עתידיים מוסמכים. ה-qualified future spike שוקל סף כמות באופק (bucket יומי). למשל, נכלל כשהביקוש ≥50 יחידות (סף) ביום בודד ובאופק שבוע.

**5. ביצוע נראה ושיתופי (Visible and Collaborative Execution):** המתכנן ממיר הזמנות מוצעות להזמנות רכש/ייצור/stock transport. משתמש בהתראות lead time/סנכרון. ‏DDR הוא pull system מבוסס-עדיפות המתריע ויזואלית. (Figure 14.8 — עדיפות לפי buffer status, לא לפי due date.)

sections.title: Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Setup
sections.en: 14.4 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Setup The first three sections of this chapter discussed DDR concepts in detail and laid the foundations that will form the basis of mapping these DDR concepts with actual setup in the SAP S/4HANA system, which we discuss in detail in the following sections. 14.4 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Setup To begin with, this section will focus on configuration settings to explain how they impact DDR master data and even business processes. Then, we’ll discuss setting up the minimal DDR-specific master data to get the DDR process up and running in the system. Next, we’ll cover some transactions or real-time business processes that DDR takes into consideration to calculate its own set of parameters. These parameters calculate the three difference zones (green, yellow, and red) and set up the right classifications (ABC, EFG, PQR, XYZ, etc.). 3 Dynamic adjustments Replenish Planning by Planning Priority The Replenish Planning by Planning Priority app is used to evaluate which products are below the reorder point. 4 Demand-driven planning MRP Run This creates receipt ele- ments. Replenishment Execution by On-Hand Status With the Replenishment Execution by On-Hand Sta- tus app, a materials planner can check for which products the on-hand stock can’t cover the buffer and expe- dite the supply. 5 Visible and collabo- rative execution Planner Overview Projected On-Hand Alerts The Planner Overview app helps materials planners find DDMRP-related KPIs so they can take action and prevent supply chain problems. The Projected On-Hand Alerts app identifies situations where the projected stock within the decoupled lead time will not be sufficient to cover all the requirements. DDMRP Components DDMRP Component Descriptions DDR Apps in SAP S/4HANA Functionalities of DDR App Table 14.1 DDMRP Components Mapping with DDR Apps in SAP S/4HANA (Cont.) 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 786 As the entire DDR process is embedded in various stages of the logistics and supply chain—such as procurement, production, distribution, and sales—it’s best that all rele- vant stakeholders gain a better understanding of an end-to-end DDR process flow. Let’s discuss configuration settings first.

sections.title: Configuration Settings
sections.en: 14.4.1 Configuration Settings The configuration settings related to DDR are buffer profile, key terms, MRP type, and lot sizing, and these are discussed in the following sections. Buffer Profile According to the DDMRP principles, products must first be classified according to vari- ous classifications, such as the usage value (the ABC classification), lead time (the EFG classification), BOM usage (the PQR classification), and variability (the XYZ classifica- tion). Depending on the settings of the variability and the lead time classification made in a buffer profile, SAP S/4HANA will determine a variability factor (VF) and a lead time fac- tor (LT factor). Both of these factors are predetermined in a buffer profile and are used to calculate the buffer. Figure 14.9 shows the standard buffer profile delivered by SAP S/4HANA, which can be found in the Buffer Profile Maintenance app. Alternatively, the buffer profile can also be accessed using Transaction PPH_DD_BUF_PROF in the SAP S/4HANA system. Figure 14.9 Standard Buffer Profile Let’s consider an example of how the system determines the VF and the LT factor from the buffer profile. For a material purchased externally (referred to as Buy) with a low variability indicator and a short lead time, the VF is 0.30 and the LT factor is 0.80. This is noted on the first row of the buffer profile in Figure 14.9. © 787 14.4 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Setup If necessary, you can create a new buffer profile with adjusted factors or assign a differ- ent buffer to each plant (in this case, Plant 1710, as shown in Figure 14.10). We will use Plant 1710 as an example throughout this chapter. Figure 14.10 Plant-Specific Settings of Buffer Profile The next section discusses some of the key DDR terms, which are helpful to refer to when considering Figure 14.9 and Figure 14.10. Key Terms The following list contains some important DDR terms and their meanings. These terms are either defined in supply chain associations, such as the Association for Sup- ply Chain Management, or by the Demand-Driven Institute:  Item type This categorizes various material types, such as procured (P), intermediate (I), semi- finished (SF), manufactured (M), and distributed (D). In the SAP S/4HANA buffer pro- file, procured materials are referred to as Buy, the produced components are referred to as Make, and the interplant transfer (stock transport orders) of materials are referred to as Transfer.  Average daily usage (ADU) This is the average consumption of a material in a given time period.  Minimum order quantity (MOQ) This is the minimum procurement quantity imposed by the supplier or the minimum production quantity or economic order quantity of a material. In SAP S/4HANA, this information is maintained in the Minimum Lot Size field in the MRP1 view of a material master.  Imposed or desired order cycle (DOC) This is the frequency of procuring a material, either imposed from the supplier side or a company’s own ordering cycle.  Decoupled lead time (DLT) This is the longest but reduced unprotected or unbuffered lead time in the BOM to procure or produce a material. In SAP S/4HANA, this information is maintained or updated in the Total Replenishment Lead Time field of a material master (in the MRP 3 view of a material master). 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 788  Lead time factor (LT factor) This denotes a factor in the lead time to procure or produce a material in the range of 0.0–1.0. Longer lead times will have smaller LT factors and vice versa. Materials planners should mutually agree to define the lead time categories (long, medium, and short) and then assign an LT factor to each lead time category. Here’s an exam- ple: – Long lead time: LT factor = 0.20 – Medium lead time: LT factor = 0.50 – Short lead time: LT factor = 0.85  Variability factor (VF) This denotes the demand or supply variability of materials in the range of 0.0–1.0. Higher variability in demand or supply will have a higher VF and vice versa. Materi- als planners should mutually agree to define the VF categories (stable, intermittent, and unstable/unpredictable demand/supply) and then assign a VF to each category. Here’s an example: – Erratic supply/demand (high variability): VF = 0.85 – Semi-stable supply/demand (significantly high variability): VF = 0.70 – Mostly stable supply/demand (medium variability): VF = 0.30  Buffer profile This is a logical grouping of materials that share similar characteristics, such as materials being procured, manufactured, or distributed across warehouses. The buf- fer profile also mentions the LT factor and VF of each material. A buffer profile con- sists of an item part, a lead time category (and an LT factor), and a variability cate- gory (and a VF). For example, a buffer profile of M, M (0.4), L (0.33) means the follow- ing: – The part is manufactured (M). – The part has a medium lead time (M) with an LT factor (0.4). – The part has low (L) demand/supply variability with a VF (0.33).  On-hand alert threshold This is defined as a percentage of the safety stock and is maintained in the Buffer Profile Maintenance app (refer to the last column of Figure 14.10). For example, if the safety stock of a material is 1,000 PC and an on-hand alert threshold is maintained as 0.10 in the buffer profile, then the system will issue a red alert in the Replenish- ment Execution by On-Hand Alert app as soon as the stock falls to 100 or below (1,000 × 0.10 = 100 PC).  Spike horizon The spike horizon is a time window that starts the day after today and comprises the DLT multiplied by a factor called the spike horizon DLT multiplier (SHT), with the addition of an offset called the spike horizon constant. The idea is that DDR will also © 789 14.4 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Setup react to a demand within this time window to ensure product availability. Referring to Figure 14.10 again, and as an example, the Spike Horizon Constant is maintained as 5.00 (days), while the Spike Horizon DLT Multiplier is maintained as 0.50. Now, if the DLT calculated by the DDR process is eight days, then the calculation for Spike Horizon is Spike horizon = 5 (spike horizon constant) + (8 (DLT) × 0.5) = 9 days.  Spike threshold DDR won’t react to all the demand within the spike horizon but only to qualified demands. To be considered a qualified demand, a requirement quantity must be greater than the spike threshold, which is calculated by multiplying the safety stock by the spike threshold factor. Only those highlighted demands will be considered qualified demands because they are within the spike horizon and above the spike threshold. Let’s explore this with an example: A safety stock (red zone) of 1,000 is calculated by the DDR process. A qualified spike demand of 1,500 is taken into account by DDR because it’s greater than the order spike threshold of 1,500. An order spike threshold is a multiplication of the safety stock (in this example, 1,000) by the Spike Threshold (1.50) as defined in the buffer profile (refer to Figure 14.10). There- fore, 1,000 × 1.5 = 1,500, which is the order spike threshold. So, any sales order with quantity of 1,500 or more and that is within the spike horizon (nine days; see previ- ous bullet point) is considered a qualified demand. Material Requirements Planning Type DDR uses the MRP type D1 that has Firming Type 1—Automatic Firming and Order Pro- posals Rescheduled Out. This setting entails that any existing planned order that lies within the time fence will be automatically considered firm and won’t be changed by MRP. If there is a shortage within the time fence, a new planned order will be created, but it will be rescheduled out (i.e., it will be created outside the time fence). As soon as this newly created planned order falls within the planning time fence, the system will automatically firm it. If the planning time fence is 15 days, then in a stock/requirements list (Transaction MD04), the MRP results when using MRP type P1 will uniquely identify the End of Plan- ning Time Fence when this 15-day period ends. A DDMRP type can be any MRP type with MRP procedure C, such as the standard MRP type D1, which will be used throughout this chapter. A DDMRP type acts like a reorder point MRP type, wherein the yellow buffer zone is the reorder point, the green zone represents the maximum stock level, and the safety stock is the red zone. Note MRP type D1 can not only be used in discrete manufacturing but also in process manu- facturing. For repetitive manufacturing, you should use the new MRP type D2 available in SAP S/4HANA 2023. 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 790 Lot Sizing A lot sizing procedure defines the rules for the quantity of the replenishment proposal created by MRP. The lot sizing procedures available in SAP S/4HANA can be grouped into the following categories:  Static lot sizing procedures  Period lot sizing procedures  Optimum lot sizing procedures DDR belongs to the static lot sizing procedures, in which the quantity will be calculated according to the quantity specifications defined in the material master. To achieve the correct MRP results for DDR, it’s also important to choose a lot sizing procedure that will replenish up to the maximum stock level after covering the requirements. For this, standard lot sizing procedure HB (replenish up to maximum stock level) is available in the system. Positioning a buffer for a product in DDR entails selecting a DDMRP type, such as the standard MRP type D1, as well as using standard lot sizing procedure HB so that MRP can correctly replenish up to the maximum stock level. Technically, these settings can be made directly in the material master, but SAP also offers the Buffer Positioning app (discussed in Section 14.5.5), which was specially developed for this purpose. When you’re using this application, filters are available so that you can select the products to process. Those products will be listed with their respective classifications and further details, such as the lead time and the DLT. You can use this information to help deter- mine whether a buffer should be positioned or not. Note In SAP S/4HANA 2023, SAP introduced a new configuration setting (Transaction OMDQ) to allow material planners to define additional requirements for inclusion in the net- flow position (NFP) calculation using the MRP type for DDMRP procedure. Following are the additional requirements categories that you can select for inclusion in open past demand:  Purchase requisition releases of stock transfer purchase requisitions  Scheduling agreement delivery schedules for stock transfer schedule lines  Subcontracting requirements (parts to be provided to supplier for adding value to a product) of subcontracting purchase requisitions  Dependent requirements of planned orders
sections.he:
הגדרות התצורה — buffer profile, מונחי מפתח, MRP type, ו-lot sizing.

**Buffer Profile:** לפי DDMRP, מוצרים מסווגים תחילה לפי usage value (ABC), ‏lead time (EFG), ‏BOM usage (PQR), ושונות (XYZ). לפי הגדרות השונות וה-lead time ב-buffer profile, ‏S/4HANA קובע variability factor (VF) ו-lead time factor (LT factor) — שניהם בפרופיל לחישוב ה-buffer. Figure 14.9 — הפרופיל התקני, באפליקציית Buffer Profile Maintenance או Transaction PPH_DD_BUF_PROF. למשל, לחומר נרכש (Buy) עם שונות נמוכה ו-lead time קצר: ‏VF 0.30, ‏LT factor 0.80. ניתן ליצור פרופיל חדש או להקצות פרופיל למפעל (1710; ‏Figure 14.10).

**מונחי מפתח (לפי ASCM או DDI):**
• **Item type:** סוגי חומר — procured (P), ‏intermediate (I), ‏semifinished (SF), ‏manufactured (M), ‏distributed (D). בפרופיל: ‏Buy (נרכש), ‏Make (מיוצר), ‏Transfer (בין-מפעלי).
• **ADU:** צריכה ממוצעת בתקופה.
• **MOQ:** כמות רכש/ייצור/EOQ מינימלית. ב-Minimum Lot Size (תצוגת MRP1).
• **DOC:** תדירות הרכש (מהספק או של החברה).
• **DLT:** ה-lead time הלא-מוגן/לא-buffered הארוך אך המופחת ב-BOM. ב-Total Replenishment Lead Time (תצוגת MRP 3).
• **LT factor:** גורם ב-lead time בטווח 0.0–1.0. lead time ארוך → factor קטן. דוגמה: ארוך 0.20, בינוני 0.50, קצר 0.85.
• **VF:** שונות ביקוש/היצע בטווח 0.0–1.0. שונות גבוהה → VF גבוה. דוגמה: ‏erratic 0.85, ‏semi-stable 0.70, ‏mostly stable 0.30.
• **Buffer profile:** קיבוץ לוגי של חומרים דומים (נרכשים/מיוצרים/מופצים), עם LT factor ו-VF. מורכב מ-item part, קטגוריית lead time (ו-LT factor), וקטגוריית שונות (ו-VF). למשל M, M (0.4), L (0.33): מיוצר (M); lead time בינוני (M, ‏0.4); שונות נמוכה (L, ‏0.33).
• **On-hand alert threshold:** אחוז מה-safety stock (טור אחרון, ‏Figure 14.10). למשל safety stock 1,000 PC ו-threshold 0.10 → התראה אדומה ב-Replenishment Execution by On-Hand כשהמלאי ≤100.
• **Spike horizon:** חלון מחר ואילך = DLT × spike horizon DLT multiplier (SHT) + spike horizon constant. ‏DDR יגיב לביקוש בחלון. למשל constant 5.00, ‏multiplier 0.50, ‏DLT 8 → spike horizon = 5 + (8 × 0.5) = 9 ימים.
• **Spike threshold:** ‏DDR מגיב רק לביקושים מוסמכים — כמות > spike threshold = safety stock × spike threshold factor. למשל safety stock 1,000, ‏Spike Threshold 1.50 → order spike threshold 1,500. כל הזמנה ≥1,500 בתוך ה-spike horizon (9 ימים) = ביקוש מוסמך.

**MRP type:** ‏DDR משתמש ב-D1 (Firming Type 1 — קיבוע אוטומטי והצעות מתוזמנות החוצה). הזמנה בתוך ה-time fence מקובעת אוטומטית; מחסור בתוך ה-fence → הזמנה חדשה מתוזמנת החוצה, ובכניסתה ל-fence מקובעת. ‏DDMRP type הוא כל MRP type עם MRP procedure C (כגון D1) — פועל כ-reorder point: האזור הצהוב = reorder point, הירוק = maximum stock, האדום = safety stock.
**הערה:** D1 לבדיד ולתהליכי; ל-REM השתמשו ב-D2 (S/4HANA 2023).

**Lot Sizing:** שלוש קטגוריות — static, ‏period, ‏optimum. ‏DDR שייך ל-static (לפי מפרטי אב החומר). לתוצאות נכונות, בחרו שיטה המחדשת ל-maximum stock לאחר כיסוי הדרישות — תקני HB (replenish up to maximum stock level). מיקום buffer ב-DDR = בחירת DDMRP type (D1) + HB. ניתן ישירות באב החומר, אך SAP מציעה את Buffer Positioning (14.5.5).
**הערה:** ב-S/4HANA 2023, ‏Transaction OMDQ מאפשר להגדיר דרישות נוספות ל-net-flow position (NFP) ב-open past demand: ‏purchase requisition releases של stock transfer; ‏scheduling agreement delivery schedules; ‏subcontracting requirements; ו-dependent requirements של הזמנות מתוכננות.

sections.title: Master Data Settings
sections.en: 14.4.2 Master Data Settings The following sections list the critical master data setup required for the DDR process. © 791 14.4 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Setup Material Master For material master 2269 in plant 1710, the MRP Type field is assigned “D1,” while the Lot Sizing Procedure field is assigned “HB.” This material-plant combination will be used as a DDR example throughout this chapter. Meanwhile, for the sake of this example only, you should maintain the numeric values for different fields in the material master as noted in Table 14.2, which also includes the purposes they serve. Note As this is just an example, you should simply maintain any reasonable values in all stock-related fields. The DDR process will automatically calculate and update these fields based on actual material usage or consumption data, which is discussed in Sec- tion 14.4.3. Second, for all the materials that are part of the DDR process, such as raw materials, packing materials, and semifinished materials, you should maintain the relevant data in the respective material masters. Figure 14.11 shows the Demand-Driven Replenishment tab that’s available in the Stock/ Requirements List (Transaction MD04), in which the Net Flow Position is shown along with other details. The Demand-Driven Replenishment tab will only appear in the Stock/Requirements List for those materials that are DDR managed. Also, scroll to the far-right side (by sliding the gray bar located at the center of the screen to the right side) of the screen to see some more DDR classifications, such as the variability indicator and the DLT indicator, among other information. Fields in Material Master Field Values in Material Master Purposes in DDR Maximum Stock Level “500” TOG Reorder Point “100” TOY Safety Stock “50” TOR Procurement Type “E” For materials produced in-house: value “E” For procured materials: value “F” Special Procurement Type “40” To be maintained only for interplant trans- fer materials Table 14.2 Material Master Fields Maintenance for Buffers in DDR 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 792 Figure 14.11 Stock/Requirements List for DDR Material Bill of Materials A material’s BOM consists of components grouped together with the relevant quanti- ties that are needed to produce the material in the production process. For example, if vanilla ice cream is the main product, then its BOM will consist of all the ingredients (referred to as components) needed to produce it. Similarly, producing an automobile requires an engine, a chassis, a body, and a large number of other components. To create the BOM of a material, use Transaction CS01. On the initial screen, enter Material “2269” and Plant “1710” and then maintain material numbers for the individ- ual components, together with the quantity for each. Although it contains quite a num- ber of materials, only materials 2262, 2265, and 2267 are relevant to DDR (in addition to the main material, 2269). Note Although only BOM details are covered here, it’s also important to maintain the other manufacturing data, such as the routing data for discrete manufacturing (the master recipe for process manufacturing and rate routing for repetitive manufacturing) and the production version. This master data setup will ensure that the planning elements created by DDR can be successfully converted into production elements (e.g., planned orders created in DDR can be converted into production or manufacturing orders). Similarly, for procured materials, you should at least maintain a purchasing info record, which is a one-to-one procurement relationship between a material and a supplier. This master data setup will ensure that the planning elements created in DDR can be successfully converted into procurement elements (e.g., purchase requisitions created in DDR can be converted into purchase orders). © 793 14.4 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Setup For interplant transfer, you maintain the material masters in question in both the plant setting and the DDR-related setting, as already discussed in this earlier section.

sections.title: Transactions
sections.en: 14.4.3 Transactions To trigger and calculate the average daily usage (ADU) of DDR-relevant materials, let’s perform some GI and GR transactions beforehand in the system and on different dates. For example, you can do the following: 1. Receive four materials in a storage location in different quantities and on different dates in the past against the initial stock posting. 2. Issue out (consume) the materials against a cost center in different quantities and on different dates in the past so that the system can automatically determine the ADU. 3. Manually create a few sales orders for this material on different dates in the past and also in the future. 4. As DDR now also enables planning for the future to account for any forecast/pre- dicted requirements, you should maintain some values in the PIRs. Performing this step will enable the system to calculate the ADU for future consumption too. All these steps are briefly covered in the following sections. Goods Receipts/Goods Issue In this example, when the DDR and non-DDR materials are created in the SAP S/4HANA system, there are no initial stocks or any history of past receipts or consumption. To maintain some stocks of different materials on different dates in the past, you perform the GR process. Use Transaction MIGO, choose Goods Receipt from the first dropdown list, and then choose Other from the second dropdown list. Then, you ensure that movement type 561 is used for initial entry of stock balances (Init.entry of stBal.), as shown on the right- hand side of the screen. In this example, four DDR-based materials are received in a quantity of 100 each on July 15, 2024 (the Posting Date). A few more similar GR transactions are undertaken but in varying quantities and on different dates. These receipts of materials on different dates and in different quantities will enable the system to calculate the LT factor and supply VF. In a real-time, actual supply chain scenario, such GRs are undertaken with reference to purchase orders for procured materials, via production or process orders for in-house- produced materials, and via stock transport orders for interplant transfer materials. To begin GI—that is, to record consumption of materials with reference to a cost center—you make selections from both the dropdowns: choose Goods Issue from the first dropdown on the left-hand side and then select Other in the relevant options drop- down that appears. Then, make sure to use movement type 201 in the GI for Cost Center 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 794 field for consumption of materials against the cost center, as shown on the right-hand side of the screen. You can then undertake a few more similar GIs, but in different quantities and on different dates. These issuances and consumptions of materials on different dates and in different quantities will enable the system to calculate the ADU. In the real-time supply chain scenario, goods are issued with reference to production or process orders (via movement type 261), cost centers (via movement type 201), sale orders (via movement type 601), or stock transport orders (via movement type 541). Note DDMRP considers all goods movement, such as goods issue and goods receipt, during the period under evaluation. But if necessary, you can exclude certain goods issuance, such as goods issue against scrap (via movement type 551), from the DDMRP calcula- tion. To make the relevant configuration settings, you use menu path SAP IMG  Pro- duction  Demand-Driven Replenishment  Assignment of Profile for Goods Issue Selection (DD). Planned Independent Requirements You can use PIRs to project ADU in the future and allow the system to calculate a pro- jected buffer for the future. This is especially relevant, for example, if you know in advance that there will be an event that might affect product consumption, such as a marketing campaign or a seasonal increase in demand. We’ll also cover this scenario in this chapter. You can use the Mass Maintenance of Products (DD) app to define the horizon in the future for which the system will look for PIRs. To create the PIRs of a material, use either Transaction MD61 or MD64. For this example, enter Material “2269” and Plant “1710” and assign the Version as “00” (Requirements Plan). Define the Planning Horizon and the Planning period in days so that the system brings up the relevant fields for data input. Then, press (Enter) to arrive at the screen shown in Figure 14.12, which shows the day-wise future demand of material 2269 in plant 1710. Figure 14.12 Planned Independent Requirements © 795 14.4 Demand-Driven Material Requirements Planning Setup It’s important to check the box in column A (active) so that the system will consider these PIRs during the MRP run. Open Past Demand Open past demand refers to sales orders for which the delivery dates have already passed but that aren’t delivered yet. To create open past demand—that is, to create a sales order—use Transaction VA01. Enter the standard sales Order Type “OR” as well as the organizational data details, such as Sales Organization “1000,” Distribution Chan- nel “10,” and Division “00.” Then, press (Enter). Then, as shown in Figure 14.13, you enter the customer, which in this case is Sold-to Party “USCU S09.” At the item level, enter Material “2269” and an Order Quantity of “600” PC. Figure 14.13 Sales Order Although it’s not shown here, the Req. Deliv.Date (required delivery date) in this case is 07/14/2024 (July 14, 2024). This is the date that DDR will consider when evaluating both the open past demand (sales orders that aren’t partially or fully delivered to customers yet) and any future demand that lies within the spike horizon, to make them a part of the net flow equation. Next, you save the sales order, and, for this example, the system creates sales order number 5616. If there are several line items in a sales order, then the system considers the First Date field for scheduling and DDR calculation purposes. It’s important to note that DDR only consider sales orders for demand and not customer requirements (via Transaction MD81). 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 796 Open Orders Open orders are basically the production orders or process orders for in-house-produced materials, purchase orders for procurement-related materials, and stock transport orders for interplant transfer-related materials whose goods are partially delivered or not deliv- ered yet but are expected to be (i.e., open orders). To create a production order, you use Transaction CO01 (use Transaction COR1 for cre- ating a process order). On the initial production order screen that appears, enter Mate- rial “2269,” production Plant “1710,” and standard order Type “PP10.” Then, choose Con- tinue. The header data screen of the production order consists of information that is applica- ble to the entire order, such as the production order number, material number, plant, and order type. The Total Qty field is relevant, and the quantity of 100 is the open order quantity of material 2269 in plant 1710 that hasn’t been delivered yet and hence is con- sidered in the net flow equation of DDR. The Dates/Times section is equally important because these dates form the basis for when the system expects the goods to be deliv- ered to the warehouse. On the production order screen, you navigate to Components, which shows the BOM data and the components that will be used in the production process. Reservations The system has automatically created reservations for three components of main material 2269—including for components 2262, 2265, and 2267—along with relevant quantities. Movement type 261, which denotes the consumption of this component, will be recorded against this production order. Finally, as these three components are also DDR-related materials, DDR will use the net flow equation. The following sections will discuss how to run the DDR process in SAP S/4HANA to ensure that you protect throughput, classify products, calculate and update buffers, and ensure better planning and execution while also focusing on key DDR metrics and analytics.
sections.he:
להפעלה וחישוב ה-ADU, בצעו GI/GR מראש בתאריכים שונים:
1. קבלת ארבעה חומרים בכמויות ובתאריכים שונים בעבר (initial stock posting).
2. הנפקה (צריכה) מול מרכז עלות בכמויות/תאריכים שונים → חישוב ADU.
3. יצירת הזמנות מכירה בתאריכים שונים (עבר ועתיד).
4. תחזוקת PIRs (DDR מתכנן גם עתיד) → חישוב ADU עתידי.

**GR/GI:** מאחר שאין מלאי/היסטוריה, בצעו GR. ב-Transaction MIGO, בחרו Goods Receipt ואז Other, וודאו movement type 561 (Init.entry of stBal.). בדוגמה, ארבעה חומרי DDR בכמות 100 כל אחד ב-07/15/2024, ועוד GRs בכמויות/תאריכים שונים → חישוב LT factor ו-supply VF. בפועל, ה-GRs מול הזמנות רכש/ייצור/stock transport.
ל-GI (צריכה מול מרכז עלות): בחרו Goods Issue ואז Other, ‏movement type 201 (GI for Cost Center). ועוד GIs שונים → חישוב ADU. בפועל, הנפקה מול הזמנות ייצור (261), מרכזי עלות (201), הזמנות מכירה (601), או stock transport (541).
**הערה:** DDMRP שוקל את כל תנועות הסחורה; ניתן להחריג (כגון scrap, ‏movement type 551): SAP IMG • Production • Demand-Driven Replenishment • Assignment of Profile for Goods Issue Selection (DD).

**PIRs:** להקרנת ADU עתידי וחישוב buffer צפוי — רלוונטי לאירוע צפוי (קמפיין, עונתיות). באפליקציית Mass Maintenance of Products (DD) מגדירים את האופק. ליצירה: Transaction MD61 או MD64. הזינו Material "2269", ‏Plant "1710", ‏Version "00". הגדירו אופק ותקופה בימים, ‏Enter (Figure 14.12). סמנו תיבה בטור A (active) כדי שהמערכת תשקול.

**Open Past Demand:** הזמנות שתאריך האספקה עבר אך טרם נמסרו. ליצירה (הזמנת מכירה): Transaction VA01. הזינו Order Type "OR", ‏Sales Organization "1000", ‏Distribution Channel "10", ‏Division "00", ‏Enter. הזינו Sold-to Party "USCU S09", ‏Material "2269", ‏Order Quantity "600" PC (Figure 14.13). ‏Req. Deliv.Date 07/14/2024 — התאריך ש-DDR שוקל ל-open past demand ולביקוש עתידי בתוך ה-spike horizon (net flow). שמרו — הזמנה 5616. במספר שורות, המערכת שוקלת את First Date. ‏DDR שוקל רק הזמנות מכירה (לא customer requirements מ-Transaction MD81).

**Open Orders:** הזמנות ייצור/תהליך, הזמנות רכש, או stock transport שטרם נמסרו במלואן. ליצירת הזמנת ייצור: Transaction CO01 (תהליך — COR1). הזינו Material "2269", ‏Plant "1710", ‏Type "PP10", ‏Continue. ‏Total Qty 100 = כמות פתוחה שלא נמסרה → net flow. ה-Dates/Times — מתי המערכת מצפה לקבלה. ב-Components — נתוני ה-BOM.

**Reservations:** המערכת יצרה אוטומטית reservations לשלושה רכיבים של 2269 (2262, 2265, 2267). ‏movement type 261 (צריכה) יירשם מול ההזמנה. מאחר שהם חומרי DDR, ‏DDR ישתמש ב-net flow.

sections.title: Running Demand-Driven Replenishment
sections.en: 14.5 Running Demand-Driven Replenishment The main purpose of maintaining buffers is to provide a cushion against the shock of fluctuations in supply chain management and financial activity by protecting the throughput. Throughput is defined as the rate at which material exits the manufactur- ing process. Lead time is the time it takes to move through the manufacturing process, and WIP, as mentioned previously, is the amount of inventory contained between entry and exit points of the manufacturing process. Therefore, throughput = (WIP ÷ lead time). © 797 14.5 Running Demand-Driven Replenishment The following sections will discuss how to protect throughput, classify materials based on ABC, PQR, and XYZ position buffers, and classify materials based on lead time.
sections.he:
מטרת ה-buffers — כרית מול תנודות, בהגנה על ה-throughput. throughput = קצב יציאת החומר מהייצור. ‏lead time = הזמן במעבר. ‏WIP = המלאי בין כניסה ליציאה. לכן throughput = WIP ÷ lead time.
להלן: הגנה על throughput, סיווג לפי ABC/PQR/XYZ ומיקום buffers, וסיווג לפי lead time.

sections.title: Protecting Throughput
sections.en: 14.5.1 Protecting Throughput DDR builds on the same buffer concept to achieve the following two primary objec- tives:  It provides shock absorption by providing inventory, thereby ensuring the protec- tion of downstream users from fluctuations in demand and supply.  It reduces the lead time required to deliver a product by removing anything that’s upstream of the buffer from the cumulative lead time. To achieve these objectives, you undertake a series of DDR-specific steps in SAP S/4HANA, such as classifying products for variability or usage value, positioning buf- fers, and finally classifying products based on the lead time. Classification is a central step in determining the decoupling points in a multilevel BOM structure as part of the DDR approach. You valuate the planning objects’ product/ plant or product/plant/MRP areas according to their essential characteristics and then assign them to classes on this basis. This classification helps you as a planner identify the appropriate settings for each planning object, which you should select based on these characteristics. In the context of DDR, these settings are defined in a certain way. The results of classifi- cation lead to the assignment of buffer profiles in a subsequent step: buffer positioning. As a result, classification is a central building block in the planning process of the DDR approach in SAP S/4HANA. In SAP S/4HANA, classification is carried out exclusively based on SAP Fiori apps.
sections.he:
DDR בונה על מושג ה-buffer לשתי מטרות:
• ספיגת זעזועים ע"י מלאי — הגנת משתמשי downstream מתנודות.
• הפחתת ה-lead time בהסרת כל מה ש-upstream ל-buffer מה-lead time המצטבר.
לשם כך, צעדים ספציפיים-DDR — סיווג לשונות/ערך, מיקום buffers, וסיווג לפי lead time.
הסיווג מרכזי לקביעת decoupling points ב-BOM רב-רמתי. מעריכים את אובייקטי התכנון (product/plant או product/plant/MRP area) לפי מאפיינים ומקצים ל-classes. כך מזהים את ההגדרות המתאימות. התוצאה מובילה להקצאת buffer profiles ב-buffer positioning. הסיווג ב-S/4HANA מבוסס Fiori בלבד.

sections.title: Classification
sections.en: 14.5.2 Classification The Schedule Product Classification (DD) app, along with other DDR-related apps, is available to you after you activate DDR in SAP S/4HANA. These apps are available via the SAP Fiori launchpad. You need to execute some SAP Fiori apps for DDR when you start using DDR as a solu- tion, whereas you’ll use operational SAP Fiori apps for DDR on a daily basis. This section will walk you through the DDR implementation steps, beginning with classifying the products. Technically speaking, buffer positioning may take place before classification, but product classification is an important factor for you to consider when you’re decid- ing where to position a buffer, so you as a materials planner should always start with product classification. 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 798 Note Because product classification will help you identify where to position a buffer, we rec- ommend that you classify all the products that may potentially be planned with the DDR logic. After you open the app, an overview screen appears and displays the job runs of the past. Choose Create to start an application job for making the necessary settings for the classification run. The Job Template in Figure 14.14 1 is preselected, while you can maintain a user-defined Job Name to clearly distinguish the individual application jobs. Scroll down and then check the Start Immediately 2 box to begin the application job right away. To schedule an application job, choose Define Recurrence Pattern, which opens the popup shown in Figure 14.15. When you’re scheduling a new job, it’s important to first define the scheduling options that will set the job start date and the recurrence pattern. Figure 14.14 Product Classification While you’re choosing the relevant option from the Recurrence Pattern dropdown scheduling options shown in Figure 14.15, the next few fields will prompt you to main- tain the application job recurrence’s details. For this example, choose Single Run and then choose OK, and the screen in Figure 14.16 will appear. © 799 14.5 Running Demand-Driven Replenishment Figure 14.15 Scheduling Options Figure 14.16 Selection Criteria for Products After the scheduling step, the next step is to define the Selection Criteria settings that will be used to select which products will be classified in the job. Figure 14.16 shows four entries in the Product field and the relevant Plant as selection criteria, so the applica- tion job will classify all the products that meet these criteria. An important parameter included in the selection criteria is the Number of Days (Past) value. This will represent the number of days in the past during which the system will look for goods movements (goods issuances/consumptions) to calculate the ADU. In this example, the Number of Days (Past) value is maintained as “30,” so the system will look for goods issued in the past 30 days to determine the ADU. If needed, you can choose to exclude days when there was no goods issuance by checking the Exclude Non Goods Issue Days box (see Figure 14.17). Doing so will increase the ADU of the DDR materials under consideration. 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 800 Scrolling down the Selection Criteria section in Figure 14.16 will bring up the screen area shown in Figure 14.17, where you can define the thresholds for the value, BOM usage, and variability classifications. As this app analyzes material movements to determine past consumption during the specified period, you can now influence the selection of material documents that form the basis of consumption. You can influence the threshold values that are used to delimit the previously mentioned classes and maintain them as percentage values in the app, as shown in Figure 14.17. Next, you maintain the relevant classification parameters for ABC, XYZ, and PQR, as shown in Figure 14.17. Then, choose the Check button to validate all the settings you’ve made, and the message noted at the bottom of the screen will appear. Finally, choose Schedule to schedule the application job. Figure 14.17 Thresholds Settings You can make settings for three different classification procedures:  ABC analysis  XYZ analysis  PQR analysis The ABC classification evaluates the relative importance of a material/plant or material/ plant/MRP area combination in relation to the other planning objects analyzed on the basis of historical consumption. The objects are divided into three groups:  A materials Relative to all objects analyzed in a run, these have had the highest consumption value in the past.  B materials These materials have a lower proportion of total consumption than A materials. © 801 14.5 Running Demand-Driven Replenishment  C materials These materials have the lowest proportion of total consumption. For classification, the consumption value is determined on the basis of the material documents. The materials involved in the classification run are then sorted in descend- ing order according to their consumption value. An A is assigned to a planning object until the threshold value of, for example, 70% is reached cumulatively across all mate- rials of the class. The subsequent materials are then assigned a B classification until, say, the next 20% of the consumption value is reached; the remaining materials are classified as C materials. The Schedule Product Classification (DD) app can perform this analysis at the level of material/plant combinations, as well as at the level of material/ plant MRP area; other levels aren’t possible. You’ll use the Value (ABC) Classification setting to define whether a product belongs to the group of products with the largest GI value (classification A), to the intermediate group with a medium GI value (classification B), or to the group of products with the lowest GI value (classification C). SAP S/4HANA will calculate the total GI value of these products within the interval defined in the selection criteria, sort materials according to this value, and then define to which group each product belongs, according to the percentages defined at these thresholds. This means that the input for these thresholds will be a percentage, and the sum of the three values should be 100%. SAP S/4HANA will calculate the total GI value within the period; that is, it will consider both the material price and the number of issues. This means that a material with a high price but without too many GIs may have the same classification as a material with a low price and a high number of GIs. ABC analysis is therefore a way of dividing the planning objects into classes according to their value-based significance. This analysis method is now being combined with two other methods that bring in further important aspects for the identification of key characteristics, thus facilitating your goal of being able to assign optimal settings to a planning object (for example, with regard to buffer configuration). One of the two addi- tional classification methods provided by the app is XYZ analysis, which is used to assess the predictability of future demand on the basis of past consumption. Analo- gous to ABC analysis, there are three classes:  X materials These materials have the most constant consumption, so it’s assumed that future consumption can be predicted with high accuracy and that therefore, buffers for the coverage of uncertainties can be reduced.  Y materials The materials in this class have greater variation in consumption than X materials.  Z materials These materials show the greatest variation in consumption, so it’s assumed that predictability accuracy is low. 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 802 The criterion for assessing predictability is a statistical fluctuation factor called the coefficient of variation, which determines, squares, and sums up the deviation of each individual observed historical value from the mean value. This sum is then divided by the number of observed values and normalized to the mean value to obtain a relative fluctuation measure. As with ABC analysis, the app enables the maintenance of threshold limits for XYZ analysis. Unlike in ABC analysis, however, these are absolute values, not percentage val- ues. The Variability (XYZ) Classification setting will classify products according to the demand variability. Products with a classification of X will have a low variability, prod- ucts with a classification of Y will have medium variability, and products with a classi- fication of Z will have high variability. The total sum of sales orders overdue, sales orders due on the current date, and order spikes are considered as the actual demand. With the mean and standard deviation of the actual demand, a coefficient of variation is calculated. This coefficient is used as the threshold for variability: the higher the coef- ficient, the higher the variability. The last possible classification methodology within the framework of the app is the PQR analysis, which you can use to analyze the planning objects to determine how many BOMs they are used in. The reason for using this type of analysis is to find out whether there is a single use or multiple uses and thus how many recipients are rele- vant for the object. You use the BOM Usage (PQR) Classification setting to determine whether a material is used in a high number of BOMs (classification P), a medium number of BOMs (classifi- cation Q), or a low number of BOMs (classification R). The value defined for each thresh- old is basically the total number of material BOMs in which a product is used, and it will be classified accordingly. You can use the three classification methods we’ve mentioned here to classify material/ plant combinations or material/plant/MRP area combinations according to the follow- ing essential characteristics:  How important they are in relative terms in the material spectrum  How predictable the future demand is  How many objects are used You can then use these three characteristics to determine the central settings of the DDR process, mainly for the purpose of defining how these objects are controlled and whether you need to maintain inventory for them. Therefore, the results of the classi- fication will play an important role in the next step: buffer positioning. You can view a summary of the results of the classification run in the application log of the Schedule Product Classification (DD) app. You can assess the log directly on the ini- © 803 14.5 Running Demand-Driven Replenishment tial screen of the app or by choosing the Back button in the job settings overview. From the overview screen, you can access two more detailed views: 1. Job Log This shows messages that have been identified by the system during runtime. In this context, it’s also possible to filter by message types. 2. Job Details This provides the settings selected for the job, such as threshold values and selec- tions. EFG Analysis According to Replenishment Lead Times In SAP S/4HANA, another option for classifying objects is EFG classification, and it’s based on the replenishment lead time. However, before you decide how to classify an object on the basis of the replenishment lead time, you need to calculate the decou- pled replenishment lead time, which doesn’t exist at this early stage. Therefore, you can only execute this type of classification with a different app in a later process step. We’ll discuss this topic in the context of lead time determination in Section 14.5.4. The results of the classification are often used together with other information to make the previously mentioned decisions, which will play a role at a later stage. If, in addition to the mathematically deductible criteria of the classifications, you use additional cri- teria that can’t be mathematically derived to make appropriate decisions, it’s referred to as a grouping. For example, it can make sense to treat a simple standard part differ- ently from a more complex electronic part with a similar consumption behavior—that is, with comparable classification results. Classes and groups that are combined are often called clusters. After you finish the first step of product classification, the information you need to posi- tion the decoupling buffers of the DDR products becomes available. To position those buffers, you can consider the results of the previous classification to determine whether a product is a good candidate for a buffer. The product classification, however, isn’t the only factor you should consider: there are external factors, and you as a planner can also use your own experience to determine when a buffer is necessary. There are some situ- ations in which a buffer may be a good option:  A semifinished product is classified as P because it’s used in too many BOMs.  Because it’s a key component and it’s used to produce many products, it might be a good idea to position a buffer for this product, thus avoiding stock-outs that might have far-reaching effects.  The source of supply of a given component purchased externally isn’t reliable, and there are too many delayed deliveries. In this case, adding a buffer would mean that the demand for this product would be absorbed by the safety stock if there is a delay. 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 804  An important product has a long lead time for production, so any late demand arriv- ing would mean a long delay.  In an MTO scenario, a customer can’t wait for the whole total replenishment lead time to have the product delivered. In this case, adding a buffer to strategically selected components will reduce the lead time, as the demand from this customer will be absorbed by the buffer.

**EFG לפי lead time:** סיווג נוסף מבוסס replenishment lead time. אך יש לחשב תחילה את ה-decoupled lead time (לא קיים בשלב זה) — לכן באפליקציה אחרת בשלב מאוחר (14.5.4).
תוצאות הסיווג משמשות עם מידע נוסף להחלטות. שילוב קריטריונים שאינם מתמטיים = grouping. שילוב classes ו-groups = clusters. לאחר הסיווג, המידע למיקום ה-buffers זמין. גורמים נוספים — חיצוניים וניסיון המתכנן. מצבים שבהם buffer טוב:
• חצי-גמור מסווג P (בהרבה BOMים) — רכיב מפתח, מניעת stock-outs.
• מקור אספקה לא-אמין עם משלוחים מאוחרים — ה-buffer יספוג.
• מוצר חשוב עם lead time ארוך — ביקוש מאוחר = עיכוב ארוך.
• ב-MTO, הלקוח אינו יכול לחכות ל-TRLT — buffer לרכיבים נבחרים מקצר.

sections.title: Buffer Positioning
sections.en: 14.5.3 Buffer Positioning When entering this application, you use the filters to select which products will be pro- cessed. Those products will be listed with their respective classifications and further details, such as the lead time and the DLT. You can use this information to help deter- mine whether to position a buffer or not (see Figure 14.18). Furthermore, you can select materials and choose Simulate DLT to simulate the decoupled lead times of these DDR materials. Note Notice the two tabs in Figure 14.18: Positioning -Internal and Positioning-External. You can use the former to determine whether the buffer position and the buffer sizing will be internal, that is, whether it will be executed within the SAP S/4HANA. You can use the latter to determine whether it will be external—that is, executed by an external system. Figure 14.18 Unbuffered Products without Decoupled Lead Time © 805 14.5 Running Demand-Driven Replenishment You can directly buffer or unbuffer a product on the initial screen of the Buffer Posi- tioning app by choosing the Buffer or Unbuffer button (see Figure 14.18). When you select one of these options, a popup appears to select a new MRP type, the new lot siz- ing procedure, and additional DDR-related material master settings. Any changes you make here will be saved directly in the material master. From the initial screen, you can also simulate the DLT calculation for one or more products, as is done in this example and shown in Figure 14.19 in the Simulated DLT column. You can then analyze the dif- ference between the current DLT and the proposed DLT for informational purposes and even for decision-making purposes. Figure 14.19 Simulated Decoupled Lead Time The Simulated DLT column in Figure 14.19 shows that the DLT isn’t calculated for these four selected products. When you select these four products and then choose Simulate DLT, the simulated DLT (in days) will appear as shown in Figure 14.19. Before you decide whether to position a buffer for a specific product or not, you should select a specific product (in this example, it is material 2262), and navigate to the Buffer Analysis app, where extensive details are available to support you in making your deci- sion (see Figure 14.20). To navigate from the Buffer Positioning app (refer to Figure 14.19) to the Buffer Analysis app, select the relevant material, which in this example is material 2262, and choose the forward arrow icon located on the far-right side of an individual material. The screen shown in Figure 14.20 then appears. Figure 14.20 shows all the information related to the Upstream and Downstream val- ues. In this situation, upstream refers to product components, for which there are the longest path or the whole BOM. Downstream refers to product parents, for which the system displays information that is related to all the BOMs in which a product is used (see Figure 14.21). 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 806 Figure 14.20 Buffer Analysis Figure 14.21 Upstream To analyze a product with many levels of components, we recommend that you switch to the Network Graph view (see Figure 14.21), where there is a graphical representation of the upstream and downstream values and multiple display options, as shown in Figure 14.22. In Figure 14.22, it’s possible to show, for example, the longest path, the product flow, or the entire BOM and BOM usage from the first dropdown, which is located in the top-left corner of the screen. There are different options to highlight specific products in the network, such as buffered products, products under an area of responsibility (AOR), products selected as favorites, and products in one of the product classifications. The example in Figure 14.23 shows a partial view of the whole BOM of a product (2269) with the characteristic (DLT Indicator) chosen from the dropdown in Figure 14.22. The BOM components are highlighted in red, yellow, or green, depending on the BOM usage. © 807 14.5 Running Demand-Driven Replenishment Figure 14.22 Network Graph Figure 14.23 Partial View of BOM with Lead Time Variability Tips and Tricks To expand or collapse details of materials in a network, you simply select the relevant material to highlight it and then choose the relevant option, as shown in Figure 14.23. 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 808

sections.title: Lead Time Classification
sections.en: 14.5.4 Lead Time Classification The Schedule Lead Time Classification of Products (DD) app uses the DDR planning characteristics maintained in the previous step of buffer positioning to determine the DLTs. These DLTs are the basis for buffer level determination. The second main task of the Schedule Lead Time Classification of Products (DD) app is to carry out a fourth classification method: the EFG classification by replenishment lead time. Unlike the three classification methods explained earlier, this classification can only be carried out after the DDR-dispatching characteristics have been main- tained because the decoupling points aren’t available in the system at the beginning of the process. After you call up the Schedule Lead Time Classification of Products (DD) app, a selection screen appears where you can create a new analysis run. In addition to the job name and start time, it’s important for you to define the objects—for example, Product, Prod- uct Group, Plant, and MRP Controller—for which the system should perform the analy- sis. Another central setting is the horizon for historical replenishment (see Number of Days (Past) in Figure 14.24). Figure 14.24 Job Settings for EFG Analysis © 809 14.5 Running Demand-Driven Replenishment Figure 14.24 shows an overview of the possible settings regarding the classification thresholds of the EFG analysis. This app classifies the products according to the lead time (EFG) classification. Just as in the Schedule Product Classification app, the initial screen of this app will show an over- view of the jobs that are already completed, in process, and scheduled. On this screen, you can create a new job, copy an existing job, or check the results of the finished jobs. The thresholds defined here are only for the EFG classification, but a materials planner can define different thresholds depending on the procurement type. The following options are available:  DLT Threshold for Buy This is used for products procured externally—that is, with procurement type F.  DLT Threshold for Make This will be considered for products manufactured internally—that is, products with procurement type E.  DLT Threshold for Transfer This is used for products with a stock transfer special procurement type, which are supplied by means of a stock transfer from another plant. In these thresholds, you as a materials planner can define how many days is considered a short, medium, or long lead time for products manufactured, purchased, or trans- ferred. This differentiation of thresholds depending on the procurement type happens because the lead time to manufacture a product may be very different from the lead time to buy the components. In addition, you must specify appropriate thresholds for the EFG classification. This clas- sification methodology is executed for material/plant combinations with a DDMRP type based on their DLTs, which are also determined in this run together with the single- level replenishment lead times. You can use different threshold values in calendar days for in-house production, external procurement, and stock transfers. In all three cases, the materials are divided into three groups:  E materials Materials with short replenishment lead times according to the respective value definition  F materials Materials with average replenishment lead times according to the threshold value definition  G materials Materials with long replenishment lead times according to the threshold value defi- nition 14 Demand-Driven Replenishment 810 While the EFG classification and, by its very nature, the determination of the DLTs is only carried out for decoupled materials with a DDMRP type, the single-level replenish- ment lead times are determined for all selected objects, including those for which no buffering is planned. For in-house production, the system determines the production or process orders over the selected analysis horizon. For all identified objects, the time period between order creation and final confirmation is determined as a single-level replenishment lead time and then aggregated as an average value on the material/plant combination. If no element is found within the selected horizon, the system uses the in-house production time of the material master, which is independent of lot size. The procedure for external procurement is the same, which means the purchase orders within the horizon are selected accordingly, and the period between purchase order creation and the date on which the final delivery indicator is set is determined. As is true for in-house production, there is a fallback scenario for external procurement in case no element is found within the selected horizon. In this instance, the system first uses the planned delivery time of the info record or contract that the MRP run selects as the preferred source of supply according to the settings. The system uses an explo- sion with lot size 1 and the explosion date of the run. If the system can’t determine a replenishment lead time, it uses the planned delivery time of the material master. For interplant transfer materials, the system evaluates the time when the goods/mate- rials were issued from a supplying plant against a stock transport order until these goods were received at the receiving plant. The determination of the DLTs is based on the single-level replenishment lead times determined as described earlier, and it uses the multilevel sum of the longest critical path in each case. The system also delivers an active BAdI implementation that enables the automated maintenance of the values in the material master. Maintenance takes place in the mas- ter data fields that were specified previously as a fallback option for determining replenishment lead times—that is, into the lot-size-independent in-house-production time for in-house production and into the planned delivery time of the preferred source of supply or the material master in the case of external procurement. The DLT is updated in the Tot. Repl. Lead Time (total replenishment lead time) field (in the MRP 3 view) of the material master.
